summary: The paper's displayed numbers largely match its text (Tables 3, 4, 6, 8; Figures 2 and 4; the abstract counts). The problems are in how some claims are framed. (1) The pilot-yield statistic mixes articles and distinct openings. (2) A footnote contradicts Table 3 on how the Stord article was coded, and the 44-project base includes that article. (3) The abstract's validation headline rests on three positive articles and has no caveat. (4) The full-run counts are unvalidated. (5) The NVDB claim is generalized from one record. (6) The abstract says the data are linked to FINN listings, but the text says no linking has been done. (7) The seasonality claim and the county ranking have no displayed support. (8) The ceremony–date-precision claim is read as attention. (9) The Table 9 word-classification rule conflicts with its own example and with Figure 2. (10) The listing-trend claim crosses a data gap. Table structured extractions were bypassed in favour of page text, as advised by the parser-quality output.

The numerator '2' is therefore distinct events, while the denominators (70 hits, 34 articles) are articles. On the paper's own counts the article-level yield is 5/34 or 3/34, not 2/34. The Figure 1 caption repeats the unit mix ('2 of 70 search hits').

findings.evidence_summary: I inspected Figure 3. The endpoints (about 35% in early 2020 and about 44% at the end) are consistent with the text. But the series is roughly flat in 2020–2023 (about 35–39%) and falls to about 34% by late 2023. The first post-gap point is near 39%, so much of the rise appears as a step across the missing months, with a smaller rise afterwards. The text says only Q1 2024 is missing while Appendix A.1 and the caption say January–April 2024 are missing, so the first plotted 2024 point (Q2) lacks April. The data cannot separate trend from a level shift or composition change at the gap; the text does not mention this.
